questions.question: Which statement best captures the role of the tangent space in optimization on manifolds?
questions.choice_A: It provides a linear approximation of the manifold near a point, allowing one to compute updates in a vector space before mapping back to the manifold.
questions.choice_B: It is a global linear subspace that contains the entire manifold and enables unconstrained optimization.
questions.choice_C: It is the set of all geodesics passing through a point, used to measure intrinsic distances only.
questions.choice_D: It is the collection of normal vectors at a point, used to impose constraints via penalties.

questions.question: For the orthogonal group $O(n)$ with elements $Q$ satisfying $Q^	op Q = I$, what is a correct characterization of the tangent space $T_Q O(n)$?
questions.choice_A: All symmetric matrices $S$ such that $QS$ is orthogonal.
questions.choice_B: All matrices of the form $Q\Omega$ where $\Omega$ is skew-symmetric ($\Omega^	op = -\Omega$).
questions.choice_C: All matrices $X$ with $X^	op Q = QX$.
questions.choice_D: All matrices obtained by differentiating polynomial curves on $O(n)$ at $Q$ only.

questions.question: How does a retraction differ from the Riemannian exponential map in practical optimization algorithms?
questions.choice_A: A retraction always follows the exact geodesic, while the exponential map is an approximation.
questions.choice_B: A retraction is defined only for compact manifolds, while the exponential map is general.
questions.choice_C: A retraction approximates the exponential map locally (matching at least first-order), often at lower computational cost.
questions.choice_D: A retraction cannot preserve constraints, whereas the exponential map always does.

questions.question: Why might a naive projected gradient method underperform compared to a manifold-aware optimizer on a curved constraint set like the Stiefel manifold?
questions.choice_A: Projection increases the dimensionality of the feasible set, creating ill-posed subproblems.
questions.choice_B: Projected gradients are undefined when the feasible set is compact.
questions.choice_C: Projections eliminate curvature information by replacing geodesic motion with linear steps.
questions.choice_D: Taking a Euclidean step then projecting can cause zig-zagging and lose the descent property relative to the Riemannian metric.

questions.question: Which statement about the Cayley transform for enforcing orthogonality is correct?
questions.choice_A: For skew-symmetric $A$, the map $Q = (I - A)(I + A)^{-1}$ yields an orthogonal matrix when $(I + A)$ is invertible.
questions.choice_B: The Cayley transform maps any symmetric matrix to $SO(n)$.
questions.choice_C: The Cayley transform equals the matrix exponential for all skew-symmetric matrices.
questions.choice_D: The Cayley transform requires computing a full SVD at each step.

questions.question: What is a key advantage and disadvantage of parameterizing $Q \in O(n)$ by $Q = \exp(\Omega)$ with $\Omega$ skew-symmetric?
questions.choice_A: Advantage: linear complexity in $n$; Disadvantage: does not guarantee orthogonality.
questions.choice_B: Advantage: always stays on the manifold; Disadvantage: computing $\exp(\Omega)$ is typically $\mathcal{O}(n^3)$ and can be costly.
questions.choice_C: Advantage: preserves geodesics exactly; Disadvantage: non-invertible for $SO(n)$.
questions.choice_D: Advantage: numerically cheaper than QR; Disadvantage: requires additional constraints to ensure skew-symmetry.

questions.question: Which description of Givens rotations is accurate in the context of building orthogonal matrices?
questions.choice_A: They are rank-one updates that adjust a single row while preserving orthogonality.
questions.choice_B: They are reflections that flip signs along coordinate axes.
questions.choice_C: They are planar rotations that act on two coordinates at a time and can be composed to form an orthogonal matrix.
questions.choice_D: They are equivalent to the matrix exponential of a diagonal skew-symmetric matrix.

questions.question: Why are QR-based retractions popular for optimization on the Stiefel manifold $\{X \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times k} : X^\top X = I_k\}$?
questions.choice_A: They produce exact geodesics under the canonical metric.
questions.choice_B: They avoid any factorization and are therefore trivially parallelizable.
questions.choice_C: They require no line search and guarantee global convergence.
questions.choice_D: They are relatively inexpensive and numerically stable, mapping a tangent step back to the manifold via QR factorization.

questions.question: What is the primary invertibility caveat of the Cayley transform $Q = (I - A)(I + A)^{-1}$ for skew-symmetric $A$?
questions.choice_A: It is undefined if $-1$ is an eigenvalue of $Q$, equivalently if $(I + A)$ is singular.
questions.choice_B: It fails when $A$ has complex eigenvalues.
questions.choice_C: It requires $A$ to be low rank.
questions.choice_D: It cannot produce matrices in $SO(n)$, only in $O(n) \setminus SO(n)$.

questions.question: Which implementation detail improves numerical stability when using a QR-based retraction?
questions.choice_A: Using classical Gram–Schmidt without reorthogonalization to save flops.
questions.choice_B: Using Householder QR (or modified Gram–Schmidt with reorthogonalization) to reduce loss of orthogonality.
questions.choice_C: Avoiding pivoting in all circumstances.
questions.choice_D: Replacing QR with LU factorization.

questions.question: How is the Riemannian gradient on a submanifold related to the Euclidean gradient?
questions.choice_A: It is the Euclidean gradient scaled by the manifold’s dimension.
questions.choice_B: It is the normal component of the Euclidean gradient with respect to the constraint.
questions.choice_C: It is the projection of the Euclidean gradient onto the tangent space under the chosen Riemannian metric.
questions.choice_D: It is obtained by integrating the Euclidean gradient along geodesics.

questions.question: Which pair of properties defines a valid retraction $R$ at a point $x$ on a manifold?
questions.choice_A: $R_x(0) = x$ and $R_x$ is linear in the tangent vector.
questions.choice_B: $R_x(0) = x$ and $R_x$ minimizes the objective function locally.
questions.choice_C: $R_x(0) = x$ and $R_x$ preserves distances exactly to second order.
questions.choice_D: $R_x(0) = x$ and the differential $dR_x(0)$ equals the identity on the tangent space.

questions.question: Which set defines the (column) Stiefel manifold?
questions.choice_A: $\{X \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times k} : X^\top X = I_k\}$
questions.choice_B: $\{X \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times n} : \det(X) = 1\}$
questions.choice_C: $\{X \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times k} : XX^\top = I_n\}$
questions.choice_D: $\{X \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times n} : X = X^\top\}$

questions.question: What is a key benefit of manifold-aware optimizers (e.g., Riemannian gradient methods) compared to penalty methods for enforcing orthogonality?
questions.choice_A: They eliminate the need for gradients entirely.
questions.choice_B: They maintain feasibility at every iterate using retractions or exponential maps, reducing constraint violation accumulation.
questions.choice_C: They guarantee convergence to a global minimum on any manifold.
questions.choice_D: They avoid any line search or step size tuning.

questions.question: In practice, why can retraction-based updates outperform Euclidean steps followed by projection on curved manifolds?
questions.choice_A: Because projections are always ill-conditioned.
questions.choice_B: Because retractions use second-order information by default.
questions.choice_C: Because retractions align the update with the tangent geometry, mitigating zig-zagging and step rejection that can occur after projection.
questions.choice_D: Because retractions avoid any factorization or decomposition cost.

questions.question: Which is a notable drawback of Givens-rotation parameterizations for large-scale optimization of orthogonal matrices?
questions.choice_A: They cannot represent all of $SO(n)$.
questions.choice_B: They require computing a full matrix exponential at each step.
questions.choice_C: They force the parametrization to be non-differentiable at the identity.
questions.choice_D: They introduce ordering-dependent parameter coupling, which can slow convergence and complicate gradient-based updates.

questions.question: What is a practical computational concern when using the exponential map with a full $n\times n$ skew-symmetric matrix?
questions.choice_A: The cost of computing the matrix exponential typically scales as $\mathcal{O}(n^3)$ and can dominate runtime for large $n$.
questions.choice_B: The exponential map is undefined for skew-symmetric matrices.
questions.choice_C: The exponential map fails to produce orthogonal matrices if step sizes are small.
questions.choice_D: The exponential map requires storing $\mathcal{O}(n^3)$ parameters.

questions.question: Among common retractions on the Stiefel manifold, which has second-order agreement with the exponential map (i.e., is a second-order retraction)?
questions.choice_A: Cayley-transform-based retraction
questions.choice_B: Polar decomposition retraction
questions.choice_C: QR-based retraction (classical Gram–Schmidt)
questions.choice_D: Projection onto the manifold via SVD truncation

questions.question: For the canonical metric on $O(n)$, what is the geodesic starting at $Q$ with tangent direction $Q\Omega$ where $\Omega$ is skew-symmetric?
questions.choice_A: $Q + t\,Q\Omega$
questions.choice_B: $\exp(tQ\Omega)$
questions.choice_C: $Q\exp(t\Omega)$
questions.choice_D: $\exp(t\Omega)Q$

questions.question: When optimizing over $O(n)$ using a skew-symmetric parameter $\Omega$, how can one reduce parameter redundancy while preserving skew-symmetry?
questions.choice_A: Constrain $\Omega$ to be diagonal and learn only the diagonal entries.
questions.choice_B: Enforce $\Omega = (\Omega + \Omega^\top)/2$ at each step.
questions.choice_C: Store the full matrix and zero it below the diagonal after each update.
questions.choice_D: Parameterize only the strictly upper-triangular entries and set the lower-triangular part to their negatives.

questions.question: Which trade-off correctly contrasts QR and polar retractions on the Stiefel manifold in practice?
questions.choice_A: QR is generally more accurate but less stable than polar.
questions.choice_B: QR is typically cheaper but only first-order accurate; polar is costlier but second-order accurate and can yield better steps.
questions.choice_C: Both have identical cost and accuracy but differ only in implementation complexity.
questions.choice_D: Polar retraction fails on tall-skinny matrices whereas QR works for any shape.
